headings.title: Introduction to Palliative and End-of-Life Care
headings.content: Palliative and end-of-life care are foundational concepts in nursing that focus on improving the quality of life for patients and their families facing life-threatening illnesses. Palliative care can be initiated at the time of diagnosis and provided alongside curative treatments, aiming to relieve pain, physical symptoms, and psychological distress. As the illness progresses and curative options are no longer viable, the care transitions specifically into end-of-life or hospice care. For Nigerian nursing students, understanding this transition is crucial because cultural and spiritual contexts often dictate how families perceive terminal illness. Nurses act as advocates, educators, and compassionate caregivers who coordinate multi-disciplinary care to ensure dignity and comfort. The core philosophy centers on viewing dying as a normal, natural process rather than a medical failure. By addressing total pain—which encompasses physical, emotional, social, and spiritual dimensions—nurses help patients live as fully and comfortably as possible until the end. This requires a shift in focus from curing the disease to maximizing comfort, supporting family coping mechanisms, and preparing both the patient and loved ones for the inevitable transition.

headings.title: Physiological and Psychological Changes in the Dying Patient
headings.content: As a patient approaches the end of life, profound physiological and psychological changes occur across all body systems. Understanding these shifts helps nurses prepare families and provide targeted comfort measures. Physiologically, the cardiovascular system slows down, leading to peripheral cooling, cyanosis, and mottled skin, alongside a gradual drop in blood pressure and a weak, irregular pulse. Respiratory patterns frequently change, featuring periods of apnea alternating with rapid breathing, known as Cheyne-Stokes respirations, and a rattling sound often called the 'death rattle,' caused by an accumulation of oral and pharyngeal secretions that the patient can no longer clear. Gastrointestinal motility decreases, resulting in constipation, nausea, or bowel incontinence, while urinary output diminishes due to renal hypoperfusion. Neurologically, patients may experience altered levels of consciousness, ranging from drowsiness and lethargy to profound coma, though hearing is widely believed to remain intact until the very end. Psychologically, patients may exhibit detachment, withdrawal from the environment, or terminal restlessness. Nurses must educate families that these signs are normal indicators of the dying process, helping to alleviate fear and promote a peaceful environment for the final moments.

headings.title: Comprehensive Nursing Assessment at End of Life
headings.content: A comprehensive nursing assessment at the end of life requires a holistic approach that evaluates physical, emotional, social, and spiritual needs. Nurses must conduct frequent, gentle assessments to detect changes in pain intensity, respiratory status, level of consciousness, and skin integrity without unnecessarily disturbing the patient. Pain assessment is paramount; for patients unable to communicate verbally, nurses rely on validated behavioral pain scales, observing for furrowed brows, restlessness, or grimacing. Assessment also involves evaluating hydration and nutritional status, recognizing that forced feeding or aggressive hydration can sometimes cause discomfort, such as edema or respiratory congestion, in actively dying individuals. Furthermore, the nurse assesses the readiness of the family to accept the prognosis, identifying cultural or religious preferences that will guide the care plan. In many Nigerian healthcare settings, family dynamics heavily influence decision-making; therefore, assessing who the primary decision-makers are and understanding their support systems is critical. Documenting these findings accurately ensures that the entire healthcare team remains aligned in providing comfort-focused care and respectful communication throughout the dying trajectory.

headings.title: Symptom Management and Comfort Measures
headings.content: Symptom management and comfort measures at the end of life prioritize relief from distress rather than the reversal of disease progression. Pain is managed aggressively using prescribed analgesics, such as opioids, administered via appropriate routes (oral, transdermal, or intravenous) to maintain a steady therapeutic level. Non-pharmacological comfort measures are equally vital; these include repositioning the patient regularly to prevent pressure injuries, providing gentle back rubs, maintaining oral hygiene with moist swabs, and keeping the room well-ventilated and quiet. For respiratory secretions that cause the death rattle, repositioning the patient on their side or administering anticholinergic medications can help reduce fluid production, though suctioning should be used sparingly as it can cause distress. Dyspnea, a common and frightening symptom, can be alleviated with low-flow oxygen, positioning the head of the bed elevated, and small doses of opioids to reduce the sensation of air hunger. Nurses also manage nausea, vomiting, and anxiety with appropriate antiemetics and anxiolytics. Throughout this process, continuous reassessment ensures that interventions remain effective and that the patient experiences maximum comfort and tranquility.

headings.title: Psychosocial and Spiritual Support for Patient and Family
headings.content: Providing psychosocial and spiritual support is an essential component of comprehensive end-of-life nursing. Patients often grapple with existential distress, fear of the unknown, loss of control, and anxiety about leaving loved ones behind. Nurses offer a reassuring presence, actively listening to patient concerns and validating their emotional experiences. Families also undergo significant emotional turmoil, experiencing anticipatory grief as they watch their loved one decline. In many Nigerian communities, spirituality and religion play a central role in coping with illness and mortality; therefore, facilitating visits from spiritual leaders, pastors, imams, or traditional faith practitioners according to the patient's and family's wishes is paramount. Nurses must respect diverse cultural and religious rituals surrounding death and dying, ensuring that families have the space and privacy to pray, sing, or perform rites. Effective communication, empathy, and honesty help build trust between the healthcare team and the family. By addressing both psychological fears and spiritual needs, nurses foster a sense of peace, closure, and dignity for the patient and their support network.

headings.title: Ethical and Legal Considerations in End-of-Life Care
headings.content: Ethical and legal considerations in end-of-life care guide nurses in protecting patient rights and ensuring that care aligns with legal boundaries and moral principles. Key ethical principles include autonomy (the patient's right to make decisions about their treatment), beneficence (acting in the patient's best interest), non-maleficence (doing no harm), and justice (fair distribution of care). Nurses often encounter complex ethical dilemmas, such as decisions regarding the withholding or withdrawing of life-sustaining treatment, do-not-resuscitate (DNR) orders, and the management of terminal sedation. While euthanasia and assisted suicide remain illegal in many jurisdictions, including Nigeria, palliative sedation to relieve refractory symptoms is an accepted ethical practice when intended to reduce suffering rather than hasten death. Legal documents such as living wills or advance directives allow competent individuals to express their healthcare preferences before losing capacity, though these practices vary widely across different cultural and legal frameworks in West Africa. Nurses must advocate for the patient's expressed wishes, navigate familial disagreements with sensitivity, and maintain meticulous documentation of all discussions and decisions made with the interprofessional team, patient, and family.

headings.title: Post-Mortem Care and Supporting the Bereaved Family
headings.content: Post-mortem care and supporting the bereaved family represent the final responsibilities of the nurse when a patient passes away. Post-mortem care must be conducted with the utmost dignity, respect, and sensitivity to cultural, religious, and institutional protocols. The nurse removes medical equipment unless an autopsy is required by law or institutional policy, cleans the body, positions it supine with arms straight at the sides or across the abdomen with a pillow under the head, and closes the eyes and mouth gently. Dentures should be inserted if appropriate to maintain facial appearance. Identification tags are attached according to hospital policy before transfer to the morgue. Simultaneously, the nurse provides compassionate support to the bereaved family, allowing them private time to view the body, express grief, and perform immediate cultural or religious mourning rituals. Providing a supportive, quiet environment and offering basic comforts like water and tissues are vital. Finally, the nurse offers resources for grief counseling and bereavement support, acknowledging that the care of the family extends beyond the moment of death.
